nature-found-015.q: In an ecosystem, what role do decomposers play?
nature-found-015.a: They break down dead matter and return its nutrients, while plants bring energy in and animals pass it on by eating.

nature-eecon-208.q: Why is sustainability called a normative idea?
nature-eecon-208.a: Because it rests on what people value and want for the future.

nature-found-005.q: Which of the four kinds of ecosystem services is the base for the other three?
nature-found-005.a: Supporting services; the other three are regulating, provisioning and cultural services.

nature-found-016.q: Besides physical goods, what less tangible things count as goods from nature?
nature-found-016.a: Things like tourism and recreation, and wild genes used to improve farm species.

nature-found-012.q: What does the Natural Capital Protocol help organisations do?
nature-found-012.a: It brings existing tools together so they can include nature in their strategic and day-to-day decisions.

nature-found-027.q: What central problem does green economics aim to fix?
nature-found-027.a: Polluters not paying for the pollution they cause, for example by using tools such as a carbon tax.

nature-found-025.q: What is the leading environmental cause of disease and death?

nature-found-045.q: Which cause of market failure does environmental economics mostly deal with?

nature-found-084.q: What happens if social costs are higher than private costs and we leave things to markets alone?

nature-found-039.q: What do ecological economists reject about human-made capital?
nature-found-039.a: The idea that it can stand in for natural capital; they favour 'strong' sustainability.

nature-found-052.q: According to Malthus, why does more food raise well-being only for a while?
nature-found-052.a: Because population then grows to use it up.

nature-found-035.q: Why does this kind of externality need no policy action?
nature-found-035.a: It acts only away from the point where the market settles, so it does not misallocate resources.

nature-found-043.q: Would the world's largest industries still be very profitable if they paid for the nature they damage?
nature-found-043.a: Hardly: they would barely be profitable.

nature-found-054.a: Supply becomes very low compared with demand, mostly because of damage to the environment such as deforestation and drought.

nature-found-088.q: Why was Ithaca's passenger railway withdrawn?
nature-found-088.a: Travellers' trip-by-trip choices did not cover its costs, even though many would have paid to keep it.

nature-found-075.q: When does a pollutant become a real pollution or health concern?
nature-found-075.a: Once its concentration is high enough to do significant harm.

nature-found-056.q: Name some illnesses that air pollution makes more likely.
nature-found-056.a: Stroke, heart disease, lung cancer, pneumonia and COPD.

nature-found-081.a: Either by choice or because regulation forces them to.

nature-found-060.q: When does ground-level ozone usually peak?
nature-found-060.a: On hot summer afternoons; it is the main gas in photochemical smog.

nature-found-077.q: How do local pollutants differ from regional ones?
nature-found-077.a: Local pollutants harm areas near the source; regional ones harm areas further away.

nature-found-069.q: How have whales responded to human-made noise?
nature-found-069.a: They have changed their migration routes and calls to avoid it.

nature-econ-156.q: How is value usually measured in money?
nature-econ-156.a: As the most a person is willing and able to pay for a good or service.

nature-econ-125.q: On an indifference map, what do curves further out mean?

nature-econ-095.a: The benefit you would have had from your second-best choice.

nature-econ-147.q: Into which two parts can any price change be split?
nature-econ-147.a: A substitution effect and an income effect, which comes from the change in buying power.

nature-econ-091.a: The extra benefits of an activity with its extra costs.

nature-econ-155.q: What did Veblen mock about the mainstream view of a person?
nature-econ-155.a: That it treats a person as 'a lightning calculator of pleasures and pains'.

nature-econ-411.q: What does a perfect substitute let you do?
nature-econ-411.a: Use it in exactly the same way as the good it replaces.

nature-econ-101.q: What can ordinal utility tell us, and what can it not?
nature-econ-101.a: It can rank options, such as two ice creams beating one, but not say by how much.

nature-econ-096.q: Give some examples of explicit costs.

nature-econ-123.a: The substitution effect, by adjusting income so the person stays equally satisfied.

nature-econ-083.q: How does capital differ from raw materials or energy?
nature-econ-083.a: It is not used up in one round of production but keeps giving services over many rounds.

nature-econ-143.q: What does a point inside the production possibility frontier mean?
nature-econ-143.a: Resources are wasted or sitting idle.

nature-econ-146.q: Name a few things that can change a good's value after it is made.
nature-econ-146.a: Age, personal attachment, cultural meaning or scarcity, as with collectable cars and comic books.

nature-econ-084.a: Government-owned infrastructure such as highways, water treatment, power grids, hospitals and schools.

nature-econ-144.q: What else is the marginal rate of transformation called?
nature-econ-144.a: The marginal opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other.

nature-econ-135.q: Give typical examples of fixed and variable costs.
nature-econ-135.a: Rent, salaries and utility bills are fixed; raw materials, delivery and production supplies are variable.

nature-econ-111.q: What is the difference between a normal good and an inferior good?
nature-econ-111.a: People buy more of a normal good as income rises, and less of an inferior good.

nature-econ-344.q: Why might someone pay more for a soft drink at a luxury resort than at a local shop?
nature-econ-344.a: Because willingness to pay depends on context.

nature-econ-335.q: What happens at a market equilibrium?
nature-econ-335.a: Competition sets a price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers produce.

nature-econ-371.q: What is the difference between moving along a demand curve and shifting it?
nature-econ-371.a: A price change moves buyers along the curve; a change in anything else, such as income or expectations, shifts the whole curve.

nature-econ-385.q: What does Engel's law say about food?
nature-econ-385.a: Spending on food grows more slowly than income.

nature-econ-402.q: What is the difference between a price ceiling and a price floor?
nature-econ-402.a: A ceiling sets the most that may be charged, like rent control; a floor sets the least, like the minimum wage.

nature-econ-409.q: Why is economic profit smaller than accounting profit?
nature-econ-409.a: Because it subtracts hidden (implicit) costs as well as the costs recorded on the books.

nature-econ-364.q: Why are firms in an oligopoly called interdependent?
nature-econ-364.a: Each firm's actions affect the others and provoke reactions.

nature-econ-367.q: What do profit-seeking firms use cost curves for?
nature-econ-367.a: To decide how much to produce.

nature-econ-386.q: What does the inverse demand function tell you?
nature-econ-386.a: The highest price that could be charged while still selling a given quantity.

nature-econ-351.q: Name some indirect ways a state can grant a monopoly.

nature-econ-382.q: What does the first welfare theorem say about market equilibria?
nature-econ-382.a: They are Pareto efficient: no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.

nature-econ-373.q: On which side of a market does most of a tax's burden fall?
nature-econ-373.a: The side less able to change how much it buys or sells.
